rows.stem: In case of association, abnormal molar mass of solute will
rows.solution: Molar mass is calculated from a colligative property, and a colligative property counts PARTICLES. When a solute associates, two or more molecules join into one particle, so the solution contains fewer particles than the formula suggests. The colligative property measured is therefore smaller than expected, and since molar mass is inversely proportional to it, the calculated molar mass comes out LARGER than the true value. So in association the abnormal molar mass increases. Dissociation does the opposite, giving more particles and an abnormally low molar mass.

rows.stem: Standard electrode potential for \(\mathrm{Sn^{4+}/Sn^{2+}}\) couple is +0.15 V and that for the \(\mathrm{Cr^{3+}/Cr}\) couple is -0.74 V. The two couples in their standard states are connected to make a cell. The cell potential will be
rows.solution:
The couple with the higher reduction potential is the cathode and the other the anode:
\(E^{\circ}_{cell} = E^{\circ}_{cathode} - E^{\circ}_{anode} = (+0.15) - (-0.74) = 0.89\ \mathrm{V}\)

Subtracting a negative number is where this is usually lost — the two values ADD in magnitude. Note also that the cell potential does not depend on how many electrons each half reaction transfers, so no balancing is needed here.

rows.subtopic: General Properties of the Transition Elements (d-Block)
rows.stem: The magnetic moment is associated with its spin angular momentum and orbital angular momentum. Spin only magnetic moment value of \(\mathrm{Cr^{3+}}\) ion (Atomic no. : Cr = 24) is ________.
rows.solution:
Chromium has 24 electrons, so \(\mathrm{Cr^{3+}}\) is \(3d^3\) and has three unpaired electrons. The spin-only magnetic moment is
\(\mu = \sqrt{n(n+2)}\ \mathrm{B.M.} = \sqrt{3 \times 5} = \sqrt{15} = 3.87\ \mathrm{B.M.}\)

The formula counts UNPAIRED electrons, not total ones, which is why the configuration has to be worked out first.

rows.subtopic: Some Important Compounds of Transition Elements
rows.stem: Acidified \(\mathrm{KMnO_4}\) oxidises sulphite to
rows.solution:
Acidified permanganate is a powerful oxidising agent and takes sulphur to its highest common oxidation state. Sulphite has sulphur at \(+4\), and the product is sulphate, with sulphur at \(+6\):
\(2\mathrm{MnO_4^-} + 5\mathrm{SO_3^{2-}} + 6\mathrm{H^+} \longrightarrow 2\mathrm{Mn^{2+}} + 5\mathrm{SO_4^{2-}} + 3\mathrm{H_2O}\)
Thiosulphate would be a reduction of sulphite, peroxodisulphate requires electrolytic oxidation of sulphate, and sulphur dioxide is simply sulphite acidified without oxidation.

rows.stem: The correct IUPAC name of \(\mathrm{[Pt(NH_3)_2Cl_2]^{2+}}\) is
rows.solution:
The complex ion carries \(+2\). Inside it the two ammine ligands are neutral and the two chlorido ligands contribute \(-1\) each, so platinum must be \(+4\):
\(x + 2(0) + 2(-1) = +2 \implies x = +4\)
The name is diamminedichloridoplatinum(IV). The \(-ate\) ending in one distractor would be correct only for an ANIONIC complex, and this one is a cation.

rows.stem:
Arrange the following compounds in increasing order of their boiling points :
(i) \(\mathrm{(CH_3)_2CH-CH_2Br}\)
(ii) \(\mathrm{CH_3CH_2CH_2CH_2Br}\)
(iii) \(\mathrm{(CH_3)_3C-Br}\)
The correct order is
rows.figureNote: ILLUSTRATIVE — PRESENTATIONAL, page idx 4. Compounds (i) and (iii) are printed as 2-D structural formulae — (i) as CH3 and CH3 on diagonal bonds to a CH joined to CH2Br, (iii) as H3C-C(-CH3)(-Br)-CH3 with vertical bonds to CH3 above and Br below. (ii) is printed as the condensed formula shown. The condensed formulae in the stem are exact equivalents of the drawings, so the crop is worth attaching for fidelity but the question is fully answerable without it.
rows.solution:
Boiling point depends on the strength of the van der Waals attraction between molecules, and that depends on how much surface the molecules present to one another. All three compounds here have the same formula, so mass is not the variable — branching is. A more branched molecule is more nearly spherical, has less surface in contact with its neighbours, and boils lower.

The tert-butyl compound is the most branched, the isobutyl compound next, and the straight-chain n-butyl compound least. The increasing order of boiling point is therefore (iii) \(<\) (i) \(<\) (ii).

rows.stem: Alkyl halides undergoing nucleophilic bimolecular substitution reaction involve
rows.solution:
In an \(\mathrm{S_N}2\) reaction the nucleophile attacks from the side directly opposite the leaving group, and the bond-making and bond-breaking happen in one step. As the new bond forms, the three remaining bonds are pushed through to the far side like an umbrella turning inside out, so the product has the configuration INVERTED at that carbon.

A racemic mixture and a carbocation intermediate are hallmarks of \(\mathrm{S_N}1\), not \(\mathrm{S_N}2\), and retention of configuration happens in neither.

rows.stem: Which is the correct order of acid strength from the following ?
rows.solution:
Acidity is decided by how stable the anion left behind is. The phenoxide ion from phenol has its negative charge delocalised over the benzene ring by resonance, so it is well stabilised and phenol gives up its proton most readily. An alkoxide ion from an alcohol has no such delocalisation, and worse, the alkyl group releases electron density towards the negative charge and destabilises it — so an alcohol is a weaker acid than even water, whose hydroxide ion carries no such group.

The order of acid strength is therefore \(\mathrm{C_6H_5OH} > \mathrm{H_2O} > \mathrm{ROH}\).

rows.subtopic: Methods of Preparation of Carboxylic Acids
rows.stem: The acid formed when propyl magnesium bromide is treated with \(\mathrm{CO_2}\) followed by acid hydrolysis is :
rows.solution:
A Grignard reagent attacks carbon dioxide at its carbon, and acid hydrolysis then gives the carboxylic acid. The carbon of the carbon dioxide becomes the carboxyl carbon, so the product has ONE MORE carbon than the alkyl group of the reagent:
\(\mathrm{C_3H_7MgBr} \xrightarrow[\text{(ii) }\mathrm{H_3O^+}]{\text{(i) }\mathrm{CO_2}} \mathrm{C_3H_7COOH}\)
Propylmagnesium bromide therefore gives butanoic acid, \(\mathrm{C_3H_7COOH}\) — a four-carbon acid from a three-carbon reagent.

rows.stem: The best reagent for converting propanamide into propanamine is ________.

options.label: C
options.text: iodine in the presence of red phosphorus

rows.solution:
Converting an amide to an amine with the SAME number of carbons is a reduction of the carbonyl group, and lithium aluminium hydride in ether does it:
\(\mathrm{CH_3CH_2CONH_2} \xrightarrow[\text{(ii) }\mathrm{H_2O}]{\text{(i) }\mathrm{LiAlH_4}} \mathrm{CH_3CH_2CH_2NH_2}\)
Bromine in aqueous sodium hydroxide is the Hofmann bromamide degradation, which would give an amine with one carbon FEWER — ethylamine, not propylamine — and that is the distractor the question is built around. Hydrogen alone will not reduce an amide under ordinary conditions, and iodine with red phosphorus is a reagent for halogenating acids.

rows.stem: Which of the following statements is not true about glucose ?

options.label: B
options.text: On heating with HI it forms n-hexane.

options.label: D
options.text: It does not give Schiff's test.

rows.solution:
Three of the statements are true. Glucose is an aldohexose; prolonged heating with hydriodic acid gives \(n\)-hexane; and it does not give Schiff's test, which is one of the observations showing that no free \(-\mathrm{CHO}\) group is present in the cyclic form.

The false statement is the one about the furanose form. Glucose exists as a SIX-membered ring, the PYRANOSE form, because the C-5 hydroxyl attacks the C-1 carbonyl. It is FRUCTOSE that adopts the five-membered furanose ring.

rows.subtopic: Colligative Properties and Determination of Molar Mass
rows.stem: An unripe mango placed in a concentrated salt solution to prepare pickle, shrivels because ________.

options.label: A
options.text: it gains water due to osmosis

options.label: B
options.text: it loses water due to reverse osmosis

options.label: C
options.text: it gains water due to reverse osmosis

options.label: D
options.text: it loses water due to osmosis

rows.solution: The concentrated salt solution outside the mango is the region of higher solute concentration, so water passes OUT of the mango's cells through their semi-permeable membranes to dilute it. Losing water, the cells shrink and the mango shrivels. That movement of solvent from lower to higher solute concentration through a semi-permeable membrane is osmosis. Reverse osmosis would require an applied pressure greater than the osmotic pressure, and nothing here supplies one.

rows.subtopic: Definitions of Some Important Terms Pertaining to Coordination Compounds
rows.stem:
Assertion (A) : \(\mathrm{[Cr(H_2O)_6]Cl_2}\) and \(\mathrm{[Fe(H_2O)_6]Cl_2}\) are examples of homoleptic complexes.
Reason (R) : All the ligands attached to the metal are the same.
rows.context: For questions number 13 to 16, two statements are given - one labelled as Assertion (A) and the other labelled as Reason (R). Select the correct answer to these questions from the codes (A), (B), (C) and (D) as given below :

options.label: A
options.text: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true and Reason (R) is the correct explanation of the Assertion (A).

options.label: B
options.text: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true, but Reason (R) is not the correct explanation of the Assertion (A).

options.label: C
options.text: Assertion (A) is true, but Reason (R) is false.

options.label: D
options.text: Assertion (A) is false, but Reason (R) is true.

rows.solution: A homoleptic complex is one in which the metal is bound to only one kind of ligand. In \(\mathrm{[Cr(H_2O)_6]Cl_2}\) and \(\mathrm{[Fe(H_2O)_6]Cl_2}\) the coordination sphere holds six aqua ligands and nothing else in each case, so both are homoleptic and the Assertion is true. The chloride ions sit outside the sphere as counter ions and do not count. The Reason states exactly the definition being applied, so it is true and it is the correct explanation of the Assertion.

rows.stem:
Assertion (A) : The boiling points of alkyl halides decrease in the order : RI > RBr > RCl > RF.
Reason (R) : The boiling points of alkyl chlorides, bromides and iodides are considerably higher than that of the hydrocarbon of comparable molecular mass.
rows.context: For questions number 13 to 16, two statements are given - one labelled as Assertion (A) and the other labelled as Reason (R). Select the correct answer to these questions from the codes (A), (B), (C) and (D) as given below :

options.label: A
options.text: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true and Reason (R) is the correct explanation of the Assertion (A).

options.label: B
options.text: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true, but Reason (R) is not the correct explanation of the Assertion (A).

options.label: C
options.text: Assertion (A) is true, but Reason (R) is false.

options.label: D
options.text: Assertion (A) is false, but Reason (R) is true.

rows.solution:
Both statements are true. Boiling point rises with the size and mass of the halogen, because a larger, more polarisable electron cloud gives stronger van der Waals attraction — hence \(\mathrm{RI} > \mathrm{RBr} > \mathrm{RCl} > \mathrm{RF}\). And alkyl halides do boil considerably higher than hydrocarbons of comparable mass, because the \(\mathrm{C-X}\) bond is polar and adds dipole-dipole attraction to the van der Waals forces.

But they are answers to different questions. The Assertion compares halides WITH EACH OTHER; the Reason compares halides with HYDROCARBONS. So both are true and the Reason is not the explanation of the Assertion.

rows.stem:
Assertion (A) : The boiling point of ethanol is higher than that of methoxymethane.
Reason (R) : There is intramolecular hydrogen bonding in ethanol.
rows.context: For questions number 13 to 16, two statements are given - one labelled as Assertion (A) and the other labelled as Reason (R). Select the correct answer to these questions from the codes (A), (B), (C) and (D) as given below :

options.label: A
options.text: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true and Reason (R) is the correct explanation of the Assertion (A).

options.label: B
options.text: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true, but Reason (R) is not the correct explanation of the Assertion (A).

options.label: C
options.text: Assertion (A) is true, but Reason (R) is false.

options.label: D
options.text: Assertion (A) is false, but Reason (R) is true.

rows.solution:
Ethanol does boil higher than methoxymethane, so the Assertion is true: ethanol has a hydrogen attached to oxygen and its molecules associate, while methoxymethane has no \(\mathrm{O-H}\) at all.

The Reason names the wrong kind of hydrogen bond. The bonding in ethanol is INTERMOLECULAR, between one molecule and the next, which is what raises the boiling point. INTRAmolecular hydrogen bonding is within a single molecule and, far from raising the boiling point, LOWERS it by using up the bonding capacity internally — as in o-nitrophenol. So the Assertion is true while the Reason is false.

rows.stem:
Assertion (A) : All naturally occurring \(\alpha\)-amino acids except glycine are optically active.
Reason (R) : Most naturally occurring amino acids have L-configuration.
rows.context: For questions number 13 to 16, two statements are given - one labelled as Assertion (A) and the other labelled as Reason (R). Select the correct answer to these questions from the codes (A), (B), (C) and (D) as given below :

options.label: A
options.text: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true and Reason (R) is the correct explanation of the Assertion (A).

options.label: B
options.text: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true, but Reason (R) is not the correct explanation of the Assertion (A).

options.label: C
options.text: Assertion (A) is true, but Reason (R) is false.

options.label: D
options.text: Assertion (A) is false, but Reason (R) is true.

rows.solution:
All naturally occurring \(\alpha\)-amino acids except glycine are optically active, so the Assertion is true. The cause is that in every one of them the \(\alpha\) carbon carries four different groups — \(-\mathrm{COOH}\), \(-\mathrm{NH_2}\), \(-\mathrm{H}\) and a side chain — and so is a chiral centre. Glycine is the exception because its side chain is another hydrogen, leaving the \(\alpha\) carbon with two identical groups.

The Reason is also true: most naturally occurring amino acids do have the L-configuration. But which configuration they have is a separate fact from whether they are chiral at all — a D amino acid would be equally optically active. So both are true and the Reason is not the explanation of the Assertion.

rows.stem:
Give reasons :
(a) Cooking is faster in pressure cooker than in an open pan.
(b) On mixing liquid X and liquid Y, volume of the resulting solution decreases. What type of deviation from Raoult's law is shown by the resulting solution ? What change in temperature would you observe after mixing liquids X and Y ?
rows.solution:
(a) Water boils when its vapour pressure equals the pressure above it. A pressure cooker is sealed, so steam raises the internal pressure well above atmospheric, and the water must be heated further before its vapour pressure can match that higher pressure. The water therefore boils at a temperature above \(100\ ^{\circ}\mathrm{C}\), and since reaction rates rise sharply with temperature, the food cooks faster. The converse is what makes cooking slow at high altitude.

(b) The volume DECREASING on mixing means the molecules have been drawn closer together than they were, so the X-to-Y attraction is stronger than the X-to-X and Y-to-Y attractions it replaces. That is negative deviation from Raoult's law: the molecules are held in the liquid more tightly, fewer escape, and the vapour pressure falls below the predicted value.

Stronger attractions mean energy is RELEASED on mixing, so the process is exothermic and the temperature of the mixture RISES after mixing.

rows.stem: Define Azeotrope. What type of Azeotrope is formed by negative deviation from Raoult's law ? Give an example.
rows.solution:
An azeotrope is a binary mixture of definite composition that boils at a constant temperature and distils over without any change in composition, because its vapour has exactly the same composition as the liquid. Such a mixture cannot be separated into its components by fractional distillation.

Negative deviation from Raoult's law gives a MAXIMUM boiling azeotrope. Because the attractions between unlike molecules are the stronger, the vapour pressure is lowered, and a mixture with a lowered vapour pressure must be heated to a HIGHER temperature before it can boil. The standard example is nitric acid and water, which forms a maximum boiling azeotrope at about 68% nitric acid, boiling at \(393.5\ \mathrm{K}\) — above either pure component.

rows.subtopic: Some Important Compounds of Transition Elements
rows.stem:
Complete and balance the following chemical equations :
(a) \(\mathrm{2MnO_4^{-}(aq) + 10I^{-}(aq) + 16H^{+}(aq)} \longrightarrow\)
(b) \(\mathrm{Cr_2O_7^{2-}(aq) + 6Fe^{2+}(aq) + 14H^{+}(aq)} \longrightarrow\)
rows.solution:
(a) Permanganate is reduced to \(\mathrm{Mn^{2+}}\) in acid while iodide is oxidised to iodine:
\(2\mathrm{MnO_4^-}(aq) + 10\mathrm{I^-}(aq) + 16\mathrm{H^+}(aq) \longrightarrow 2\mathrm{Mn^{2+}}(aq) + 8\mathrm{H_2O}(l) + 5\mathrm{I_2}(s)\)

(b) Dichromate is reduced to \(\mathrm{Cr^{3+}}\) while iron(II) is oxidised to iron(III):
\(\mathrm{Cr_2O_7^{2-}}(aq) + 6\mathrm{Fe^{2+}}(aq) + 14\mathrm{H^+}(aq) \longrightarrow 2\mathrm{Cr^{3+}}(aq) + 6\mathrm{Fe^{3+}}(aq) + 7\mathrm{H_2O}(l)\)

Both are worth checking by counting electrons: in (a) manganese goes \(+7\) to \(+2\), five electrons each for two atoms, matched by ten iodides losing one each; in (b) two chromiums go \(+6\) to \(+3\), three each, matched by six irons losing one each.

rows.subtopic: Chemical Reactions of Aldehydes and Ketones
rows.stem: Would you expect benzaldehyde to be more reactive or less reactive in nucleophilic addition reactions than propanal ? Justify your answer.
rows.solution:
Benzaldehyde is LESS reactive than propanal towards nucleophilic addition.

Nucleophilic addition begins with attack on the carbonyl carbon, so the reaction is as easy as that carbon is electrophilic. In benzaldehyde the carbonyl group is conjugated with the benzene ring, and resonance pushes electron density from the ring towards the carbonyl carbon. The partial positive charge on that carbon is therefore reduced, the polarity of the \(\mathrm{C{=}O}\) group is diminished, and the nucleophile is less strongly attracted. The bulk of the phenyl group adds a steric obstacle as well. Propanal has only a small ethyl group, which offers neither the resonance donation nor the crowding.

rows.stem:
Identify A and B in each of the following reaction sequence :
(a) \(\mathrm{CH_3CH_2Cl} \xrightarrow{\ \mathrm{NaCN}\ } \mathrm{A} \xrightarrow{\ \mathrm{H_2/Ni}\ } \mathrm{B}\)
(b) \(\mathrm{C_6H_5NH_2} \xrightarrow[\ 0-5\ ^{\circ}\mathrm{C}\ ]{\ \mathrm{NaNO_2/HCl}\ } \mathrm{A} \xrightarrow[\ \mathrm{H^{+}}\ ]{\ \mathrm{C_6H_5NH_2}\ } \mathrm{B}\)
rows.solution:
(a) Sodium cyanide is ionic, so the free cyanide ion attacks through its CARBON and gives the alkyl cyanide; catalytic hydrogenation then reduces the nitrile to a primary amine with the same number of carbons.
\(\mathrm{A} = \mathrm{CH_3CH_2CN}\), propanenitrile
\(\mathrm{B} = \mathrm{CH_3CH_2CH_2NH_2}\), propylamine
Note the chain has gained a carbon at the cyanide step, so the amine has three carbons where the halide had two.

(b) Sodium nitrite in hydrochloric acid at \(0-5\ ^{\circ}\mathrm{C}\) diazotises aniline; the diazonium ion then couples with a second molecule of aniline at the position para to its amino group.
\(\mathrm{A} = \mathrm{C_6H_5N_2^+Cl^-}\), benzenediazonium chloride
\(\mathrm{B} = \mathrm{C_6H_5-N{=}N-C_6H_4-NH_2}\ (p)\), p-aminoazobenzene

rows.stem:
Write the reactions involved when D-glucose is treated with the following reagents :
(a) HCN
(b) \(\mathrm{Br_2}\) water
rows.solution:
(a) Hydrogen cyanide adds across the carbon-oxygen double bond of the aldehyde group at C-1, giving the cyanohydrin:
\(\mathrm{CHO(CHOH)_4CH_2OH} + \mathrm{HCN} \longrightarrow \mathrm{CH(OH)(CN)(CHOH)_4CH_2OH}\)
This is one of the reactions establishing that a carbonyl group is present in the open chain form.

(b) Bromine water is a mild oxidising agent and attacks only the aldehyde group, leaving the alcoholic groups untouched. The product is the six-carbon monocarboxylic gluconic acid:
\(\mathrm{CHO(CHOH)_4CH_2OH} \xrightarrow{\mathrm{Br_2}/\mathrm{H_2O}} \mathrm{COOH(CHOH)_4CH_2OH}\)
Its failure with the ketose fructose is how the two sugars are told apart.

rows.subtopic: Colligative Properties and Determination of Molar Mass
rows.stem: A solution of glucose (molar mass = 180 g \(\mathrm{mol^{-1}}\)) in water has a boiling point of 100.20 °C. Calculate the freezing point of the same solution. Molal constants for water \(\mathrm{K_f}\) and \(\mathrm{K_b}\) are 1.86 K kg \(\mathrm{mol^{-1}}\) and 0.512 K kg \(\mathrm{mol^{-1}}\) respectively.
rows.solution:
Both colligative effects share the same molality, so the boiling point elevation is used to find it and the freezing point depression then follows.

\(\Delta T_b = T_b - T_b^{\circ} = 100.20 - 100 = 0.20\ \mathrm{K}\)

From \(\Delta T_b = K_b \, m\),
\(m = \dfrac{0.20}{0.512} = 0.390\ \mathrm{mol\ kg^{-1}}\)

Then
\(\Delta T_f = K_f \, m = 1.86 \times 0.390 = 0.725\ \mathrm{K}\)

and the freezing point of the solution is
\(T_f = 273.15 - 0.725 = 272.425\ \mathrm{K}\), that is \(-0.725\ ^{\circ}\mathrm{C}\).

The molar mass of glucose is given but never needed: the molality is obtained from the measured elevation, not from the mass of solute.

rows.stem:
(a) State the following :
(i) Kohlrausch law of independent migration of ions and
(ii) Faraday's first law of electrolysis.
(b) Using \(\mathrm{E^{\circ}_{values}}\) of X and Y given below, predict which is better for coating the surface of iron to prevent corrosion and why ?
Given \(\mathrm{E^{\circ}_{X^{2+}/X}} = -2.36\) V,
\(\mathrm{E^{\circ}_{Y^{2+}/Y}} = -0.14\) V,
\(\mathrm{E^{\circ}_{Fe^{2+}/Fe}} = -0.44\) V
rows.solution:
(a)(i) Kohlrausch's law of independent migration of ions states that at infinite dilution the limiting molar conductivity of an electrolyte is the sum of the individual limiting contributions of its cation and its anion, each counted as many times as the formula unit provides it.

(ii) Faraday's first law of electrolysis states that the amount of chemical reaction occurring at any electrode during electrolysis is proportional to the quantity of electricity passed through the electrolyte.

(b) X is the better coating. A sacrificial coating protects iron only if it is oxidised in preference to the iron, which means it must have the MORE NEGATIVE electrode potential — equivalently, the greater oxidation potential. X is at \(-2.36\) V against iron's \(-0.44\) V, so X corrodes first and the iron beneath is spared, and the protection continues even if the coating is scratched. Y at \(-0.14\) V is less easily oxidised than iron, so once its layer is broken the iron would corrode preferentially and the coating would make matters worse.

rows.subtopic: Temperature Dependence of the Rate of a Reaction
rows.stem:
A certain reaction is 50% complete in 20 minutes at 300 K and the same reaction is 50% complete in 5 minutes at 350 K. Calculate the activation energy if it is a first order reaction.
[R = 8.314 J \(\mathrm{K^{-1}\ mol^{-1}}\); log 4 = 0.602]
rows.solution:
For a first order reaction the half-life fixes the rate constant, and "50% complete" is the half-life.

At 300 K: \(k_1 = \dfrac{0.693}{20} = 0.03465\ \mathrm{min^{-1}}\)
At 350 K: \(k_2 = \dfrac{0.693}{5} = 0.1386\ \mathrm{min^{-1}}\)

so \(\dfrac{k_2}{k_1} = 4\), and the given \(\log 4\) is what the question intends.

\(\log\dfrac{k_2}{k_1} = \dfrac{E_a}{2.303\,R}\left[\dfrac{T_2 - T_1}{T_1 T_2}\right]\)
\(\log 4 = \dfrac{E_a}{2.303 \times 8.314} \times \dfrac{50}{300 \times 350}\)
\(0.602 = \dfrac{E_a}{19.147} \times \dfrac{50}{105000}\)

\(E_a = 24209\ \mathrm{J\ mol^{-1}}\), that is \(24.209\ \mathrm{kJ\ mol^{-1}}\)

The minutes cancel in the RATIO of the two rate constants, so there is no need to convert them to seconds.

rows.subtopic: General Properties of the Transition Elements (d-Block)
rows.stem:
The elements of 3d transition series are given as :
Sc, Ti, V, Cr, Mn, Fe, Co, Ni, Cu, Zn
Answer the following :
(a) Copper has exceptionally positive \(\mathrm{E^{\circ}_{M^{2+}/M}}\) value, why ?
(b) Which element is a strong reducing agent in +2 oxidation state and why ?
(c) \(\mathrm{Zn^{2+}}\) salts are colourless. Why ?
rows.solution:
(a) Because the overall change from copper metal to hydrated \(\mathrm{Cu^{2+}}\) is energetically unfavourable. Copper has a HIGH enthalpy of atomisation and high ionisation enthalpies, and the hydration enthalpy of \(\mathrm{Cu^{2+}}\), although large, is NOT large enough to repay them. A positive \(E^{\circ}\) is the record of that balance — and it is why copper does not liberate hydrogen from dilute acids.

(b) Chromium. \(\mathrm{Cr^{2+}}\) is \(3d^4\), and losing one more electron gives \(\mathrm{Cr^{3+}}\), \(3d^3\), with a stable half-filled \(t_{2g}\) set. Because the oxidised form is so much more favourable, \(\mathrm{Cr^{2+}}\) gives up an electron readily, which is exactly what being a strong reducing agent means.

(c) \(\mathrm{Zn^{2+}}\) is \(3d^{10}\) — a completely filled d subshell. Colour in these ions comes from a d-d transition, in which an electron absorbs visible light and moves from the lower set of d orbitals to the upper one; with every d orbital full there is no vacancy to move into, no light is absorbed, and the salts are colourless.

rows.stem:
Draw the structure of the major monohalo product for each of the following reaction :
(a) 1-chloro-4-ethylbenzene \(\xrightarrow{\ \mathrm{Br_2},\ \text{Heat}\ }\) ?
(b) 1-methylcyclohexene + HBr \(\longrightarrow\) ?
(c) 4-(hydroxymethyl)phenol \(\xrightarrow{\ \mathrm{HCl},\ \text{Heat}\ }\) ?
rows.figureNote: REQUIRED — REQUIRED, page idx 14. All three substrates are printed as DRAWN 2-D structures, not as names: (a) a benzene ring bearing CH2-CH3 and, para to it, Cl; (b) a cyclohexene ring with CH3 on one of the doubly-bonded carbons; (c) a benzene ring bearing OH and, para to it, HO-H2C. The reagent sits above each reaction arrow and the product is a '?'. The names in the stem are the maintainer's reading of those drawings (permitted by the addendum: naming a compound in words is text); the crop is the faithful record.
rows.solution:
(a) Bromine with heat attacks the side chain rather than the ring, taking the BENZYLIC hydrogen because the radical formed there is stabilised by the ring. In 1-chloro-4-ethylbenzene that is the \(\mathrm{CH_2}\) carbon:
\(\mathrm{4\text{-}Cl{-}C_6H_4{-}CH_2CH_3} + \mathrm{Br_2} \xrightarrow{\Delta} \mathrm{4\text{-}Cl{-}C_6H_4{-}CHBr{-}CH_3}\)
The product is 1-chloro-4-(1-bromoethyl)benzene.

(b) Addition of \(\mathrm{HBr}\) follows Markovnikov's rule: the proton goes to the alkene carbon carrying more hydrogens, so the more stable carbocation forms. In 1-methylcyclohexene the substituted ring carbon has none and its neighbour has one, so the bromide ends up on the carbon bearing the methyl group. The product is 1-bromo-1-methylcyclohexane, a tertiary halide.

(c) The molecule has two hydroxyl groups and only one reacts. The benzylic ALCOHOLIC \(-\mathrm{OH}\) is replaced by chlorine; the PHENOLIC \(-\mathrm{OH}\) is not, because its oxygen lone pair is delocalised into the ring and the \(\mathrm{C-O}\) bond has partial double bond character too strong for hydrogen chloride to break.
\(\mathrm{HO{-}C_6H_4{-}CH_2OH} + \mathrm{HCl} \xrightarrow{\Delta} \mathrm{HO{-}C_6H_4{-}CH_2Cl} + \mathrm{H_2O}\)
The product is 4-(chloromethyl)phenol.

rows.stem:
How do you convert :
(a) Chlorobenzene to biphenyl
(b) Propene to 1-Iodopropane
(c) 2-bromobutane to but-2-ene.
rows.solution:
(a) Chlorobenzene to biphenyl. This is the Fittig reaction: sodium in dry ether couples two aryl halide units through the carbons that carried the halogen.
\(2\mathrm{C_6H_5Cl} + 2\mathrm{Na} \xrightarrow{\text{dry ether}} \mathrm{C_6H_5-C_6H_5} + 2\mathrm{NaCl}\)

(b) Propene to 1-iodopropane, in two steps. The iodine must end up on the TERMINAL carbon, so the first addition has to be anti-Markovnikov: hydrogen bromide in the presence of a peroxide gives 1-bromopropane. Finkelstein exchange with sodium iodide in dry acetone then swaps the bromine for iodine, the insoluble sodium bromide precipitating and driving the reaction forward.
\(\mathrm{CH_3CH{=}CH_2} \xrightarrow[\text{peroxide}]{\mathrm{HBr}} \mathrm{CH_3CH_2CH_2Br} \xrightarrow[\text{dry acetone}]{\mathrm{NaI}} \mathrm{CH_3CH_2CH_2I}\)

(c) 2-Bromobutane to but-2-ene. Alcoholic potassium hydroxide acts as a base and eliminates; by Saytzeff's rule the more substituted alkene predominates.
\(\mathrm{CH_3CHBrCH_2CH_3} + \mathrm{KOH\ (alc.)} \xrightarrow{\Delta} \mathrm{CH_3CH{=}CHCH_3} + \mathrm{KBr} + \mathrm{H_2O}\)

rows.stem:
(a) Arrange the following compounds in increasing order of their boiling point :
\(\mathrm{(CH_3)_2NH}\), \(\mathrm{CH_3CH_2NH_2}\), \(\mathrm{CH_3CH_2OH}\).
(b) Give plausible explanation for each of the following :
(i) Aromatic primary amines cannot be prepared by Gabriel Phthalimide synthesis.
(ii) Amides are less basic than amines.
rows.solution:
(a) Boiling point rises with the strength of intermolecular hydrogen bonding. A tertiary-style secondary amine, \((\mathrm{CH_3})_2\mathrm{NH}\), has only ONE hydrogen on nitrogen, so it forms the fewest hydrogen bonds. Ethylamine has two hydrogens on nitrogen and forms more. Ethanol has its hydrogen on OXYGEN, which is more electronegative than nitrogen, so its hydrogen bonds are the strongest of the three. The increasing order is
\((\mathrm{CH_3})_2\mathrm{NH} < \mathrm{CH_3CH_2NH_2} < \mathrm{CH_3CH_2OH}\)

(b)(i) Gabriel phthalimide synthesis works by having the phthalimide anion displace a halide by nucleophilic substitution. Aryl halides do not undergo that substitution: the \(\mathrm{C-X}\) bond has partial double bond character from resonance with the ring, and the electron-rich ring repels the incoming nucleophile. The first step therefore never happens, and aromatic primary amines cannot be made this way.

(ii) In an amide the nitrogen lone pair is delocalised onto the carbonyl oxygen by resonance, so it is not freely available to accept a proton. In an amine no such delocalisation exists and the lone pair sits on nitrogen ready to be donated. Protonating an amide also destroys that stabilising resonance, which costs energy. Amides are therefore much less basic than amines.

rows.stem:
(a) What is the difference between native protein and denatured protein ?
(b) Which one of the following is a disaccharide ?
Glucose, Lactose, Amylose, Fructose
(c) Which vitamin is responsible for the coagulation of blood ?
rows.solution:
(a) A NATIVE protein has its three-dimensional structure intact — the secondary and tertiary folding is in place — and it is biologically active. A DENATURED protein has had that three-dimensional structure destroyed by heat or by a change in pH, and it is biologically inactive. The primary structure, the sequence of residues, survives in both, since denaturation does not break peptide bonds.

(b) Lactose. Glucose and fructose are monosaccharides and amylose is a polysaccharide; lactose is the disaccharide, made of one glucose and one galactose unit.

(c) Vitamin K is responsible for the coagulation of blood; its deficiency causes increased clotting time.

rows.subtopic: Factors Influencing Rate of a Reaction
rows.stem:
(i) What is a rate determining step ?
(ii) Define complex reaction.
rows.context: The rate of a chemical reaction is expressed either in terms of decrease in the concentration of reactants or increase in the concentration of a product per unit time. Rate of the reaction depends upon the nature of reactants, concentration of reactants, temperature, presence of catalyst, surface area of the reactants and presence of light. Rate of reaction is directly related to the concentration of reactant. Rate law states that the rate of reaction depends upon the concentration terms on which the rate of reaction actually depends, as observed experimentally. The sum of powers of the concentration of the reactants in the Rate law expression is called order of reaction while the number of reacting species taking part in an elementary reaction which must collide simultaneously in order to bring about a chemical reaction is called molecularity of the reaction.
rows.solution:
(i) The rate determining step is the SLOWEST step in the mechanism of a complex reaction. Because the overall reaction can go no faster than its slowest stage, this step governs the observed rate, and the rate law — and hence the order — is read from it.

(ii) A complex reaction is one that proceeds through a SERIES of elementary reactions, that is through two or more steps, rather than in a single step. Its overall balanced equation describes only the net change and not the mechanism, which is why its order cannot be predicted from that equation.

rows.subtopic: Temperature Dependence of the Rate of a Reaction
rows.stem: What is the effect of temperature on the rate constant of a reaction ?
rows.context: The rate of a chemical reaction is expressed either in terms of decrease in the concentration of reactants or increase in the concentration of a product per unit time. Rate of the reaction depends upon the nature of reactants, concentration of reactants, temperature, presence of catalyst, surface area of the reactants and presence of light. Rate of reaction is directly related to the concentration of reactant. Rate law states that the rate of reaction depends upon the concentration terms on which the rate of reaction actually depends, as observed experimentally. The sum of powers of the concentration of the reactants in the Rate law expression is called order of reaction while the number of reacting species taking part in an elementary reaction which must collide simultaneously in order to bring about a chemical reaction is called molecularity of the reaction.
rows.solution: The rate constant increases with increasing temperature. Raising the temperature widens the distribution of molecular energies and greatly increases the fraction of molecules carrying energy equal to or above the activation energy, and the Arrhenius equation \(k = Ae^{-E_a/RT}\) records that: as \(T\) rises, the exponent becomes less negative and \(k\) grows. As a rough rule, a rise of \(10\ \mathrm{K}\) near room temperature roughly doubles the rate constant.

rows.subtopic: Factors Influencing Rate of a Reaction
rows.stem: Why is molecularity applicable only for elementary reactions whereas order is applicable for elementary as well as complex reactions ?
rows.context: The rate of a chemical reaction is expressed either in terms of decrease in the concentration of reactants or increase in the concentration of a product per unit time. Rate of the reaction depends upon the nature of reactants, concentration of reactants, temperature, presence of catalyst, surface area of the reactants and presence of light. Rate of reaction is directly related to the concentration of reactant. Rate law states that the rate of reaction depends upon the concentration terms on which the rate of reaction actually depends, as observed experimentally. The sum of powers of the concentration of the reactants in the Rate law expression is called order of reaction while the number of reacting species taking part in an elementary reaction which must collide simultaneously in order to bring about a chemical reaction is called molecularity of the reaction.
rows.solution:
The two quantities come from different places, and that is the whole answer.

MOLECULARITY counts the number of species that must collide SIMULTANEOUSLY in a single step, so it is defined only where there is a single step to look at — an elementary reaction. A complex reaction is a sequence of elementary steps, each with its own molecularity, and there is no single number for the reaction as a whole.

ORDER is obtained from the EXPERIMENTALLY determined rate law, and every reaction, however many steps it has, has a measurable rate law. So order is meaningful for both. For a complex reaction the rate law comes from the slowest step, which is why order can even be fractional — something molecularity, being a count of molecules, can never be.

rows.subtopic: Factors Influencing Rate of a Reaction
rows.stem: The conversion of molecule X to Y follows second order kinetics. If concentration of X is increased 3 times, how will it affect the rate of formation of Y ?
rows.context: The rate of a chemical reaction is expressed either in terms of decrease in the concentration of reactants or increase in the concentration of a product per unit time. Rate of the reaction depends upon the nature of reactants, concentration of reactants, temperature, presence of catalyst, surface area of the reactants and presence of light. Rate of reaction is directly related to the concentration of reactant. Rate law states that the rate of reaction depends upon the concentration terms on which the rate of reaction actually depends, as observed experimentally. The sum of powers of the concentration of the reactants in the Rate law expression is called order of reaction while the number of reacting species taking part in an elementary reaction which must collide simultaneously in order to bring about a chemical reaction is called molecularity of the reaction.
rows.solution:
Second order kinetics means rate \(= k[\mathrm{X}]^2\). Tripling the concentration of X therefore multiplies the rate by \(3^2\):
\(\text{new rate} = k(3[\mathrm{X}])^2 = 9\,k[\mathrm{X}]^2\)
The rate of formation of Y becomes 9 times what it was.

rows.stem:
What happens when phenol reacts with
(i) \(\mathrm{Br_2/CS_2}\)
(ii) Conc. \(\mathrm{HNO_3}\)
rows.context: Phenols undergo electrophilic substitution reactions readily due to the strong activating effect of OH group attached to the benzene ring. Since, the OH group increases the electron density more to o– and p– positions therefore OH group is ortho, para-directing. Reimer-Tiemann reaction is one of the examples of aldehyde group being introduced on the aromatic ring of phenol, ortho to the hydroxyl group. This is a general method used for the ortho-formylation of phenols.
rows.solution:
(i) In a non-polar solvent such as carbon disulphide, and at low temperature, phenol is not ionised, so the ring is activated but only moderately and a single bromine enters. It enters at both available activated positions, so the product is a mixture of 2-bromophenol and 4-bromophenol, separated afterwards by distillation.
\(\mathrm{C_6H_5OH} \xrightarrow[273\ \mathrm{K}]{\mathrm{Br_2}/\mathrm{CS_2}} \text{2-bromophenol} + \text{4-bromophenol}\)

(ii) Concentrated nitric acid nitrates all three available positions at once, giving 2,4,6-trinitrophenol, better known as picric acid.
\(\mathrm{C_6H_5OH} \xrightarrow{\text{conc. }\mathrm{HNO_3}} \mathrm{2,4,6\text{-}(O_2N)_3{-}C_6H_2{-}OH}\)
The contrast between the two is the point: the same ring, and how far the substitution goes depends entirely on the conditions.

rows.stem: Why phenol does not undergo protonation readily ?
rows.context: Phenols undergo electrophilic substitution reactions readily due to the strong activating effect of OH group attached to the benzene ring. Since, the OH group increases the electron density more to o– and p– positions therefore OH group is ortho, para-directing. Reimer-Tiemann reaction is one of the examples of aldehyde group being introduced on the aromatic ring of phenol, ortho to the hydroxyl group. This is a general method used for the ortho-formylation of phenols.
rows.solution: Protonation means the oxygen must donate a lone pair to a proton. In phenol that lone pair is not sitting free: it is delocalised into the benzene ring by resonance, which is what activates the ring towards electrophiles in the first place. Because the electron pair is spread over the ring rather than localised on oxygen, it is much less available for donation, and phenol is protonated far less readily than an alcohol. The same delocalisation is also what gives the \(\mathrm{C-O}\) bond of phenol its partial double bond character.

rows.stem: Which is a stronger acid - phenol or cresol ? Give reason.
rows.context: Phenols undergo electrophilic substitution reactions readily due to the strong activating effect of OH group attached to the benzene ring. Since, the OH group increases the electron density more to o– and p– positions therefore OH group is ortho, para-directing. Reimer-Tiemann reaction is one of the examples of aldehyde group being introduced on the aromatic ring of phenol, ortho to the hydroxyl group. This is a general method used for the ortho-formylation of phenols.
rows.solution:
Phenol is the stronger acid.

Acidity is decided by how stable the phenoxide ion is once the proton has left. Cresol carries a methyl group on the ring, and a methyl group releases electron density by the \(+I\) effect. Pushing electron density towards an already negative phenoxide ion destabilises it, so cresol holds its proton more tightly. Phenol has no such group, its phenoxide is the better stabilised of the two, and it is therefore the stronger acid. Electron-WITHDRAWING substituents work the other way, which is why nitrophenols are stronger acids than phenol.

rows.stem: Write the IUPAC name of the product formed in the Reimer-Tiemann reaction.
rows.context: Phenols undergo electrophilic substitution reactions readily due to the strong activating effect of OH group attached to the benzene ring. Since, the OH group increases the electron density more to o– and p– positions therefore OH group is ortho, para-directing. Reimer-Tiemann reaction is one of the examples of aldehyde group being introduced on the aromatic ring of phenol, ortho to the hydroxyl group. This is a general method used for the ortho-formylation of phenols.
rows.solution: The Reimer-Tiemann reaction converts phenol into salicylaldehyde, whose IUPAC name is 2-hydroxybenzaldehyde. Phenol is treated with chloroform and aqueous sodium hydroxide, which generate dichlorocarbene; this attacks the ring at the position ortho to the \(-\mathrm{OH}\), and acidification of the intermediate gives the aldehyde.

rows.stem:
(a) Write the cell reaction and calculate the e.m.f. of the following cell at 298 K :
\(\mathrm{Sn(s) \mid Sn^{2+}\ (0.004\ M) \parallel H^{+}\ (0.02\ M) \mid H_2(g)\ (1\ Bar) \mid Pt\ (s)}\)
(Given : \(\mathrm{E^{\circ}_{Sn^{2+}/Sn}} = -0.14\) V, \(\mathrm{E^{\circ}_{H^{+}\mid H_2(g),\ Pt}} = 0.00\) V)
(b) Account for the following ;
(i) On the basis of \(\mathrm{E^{\circ}}\) values, \(\mathrm{O_2}\) gas should be liberated at anode but it is \(\mathrm{Cl_2}\) gas which is liberated in the electrolysis of aqueous NaCl.
(ii) Conductivity of \(\mathrm{CH_3COOH}\) decreases on dilution.
rows.solution:
(a) Tin is written on the left, so it is the anode and is oxidised; the hydrogen electrode is the cathode. The cell reaction is
\(\mathrm{Sn(s)} + 2\mathrm{H^+}(aq) \longrightarrow \mathrm{Sn^{2+}}(aq) + \mathrm{H_2(g)}\)
so two electrons are transferred and \(n = 2\).

\(E^{\circ}_{cell} = E^{\circ}_{\mathrm{H^+/H_2}} - E^{\circ}_{\mathrm{Sn^{2+}/Sn}} = 0 - (-0.14) = 0.14\ \mathrm{V}\)

Hydrogen is at 1 bar so its pressure term is 1 and drops out:
\(E_{cell} = E^{\circ}_{cell} - \dfrac{0.059}{2}\log\dfrac{[\mathrm{Sn^{2+}}]}{[\mathrm{H^+}]^2}\)
\(= 0.14 - \dfrac{0.059}{2}\log\dfrac{0.004}{(0.02)^2} = 0.14 - 0.0295\log 10\)
\(= 0.14 - 0.0295 = 0.1105\ \mathrm{V}\)

(b)(i) Because of the OVERPOTENTIAL of oxygen. The standard potentials say water should be oxidised in preference to chloride, but releasing a gas on a real electrode requires an extra voltage over and above the thermodynamic value, and for oxygen that extra requirement is large. It raises the effective voltage needed for oxygen above that needed for chlorine, so chlorine appears instead. This is a case where thermodynamics alone predicts the wrong product and the electrode kinetics decide it.

(ii) Conductivity, \(\kappa\), is the conductance of a unit VOLUME of solution, so it depends on how many ions that volume contains. Diluting a solution spreads the same ions through a larger volume, so any given volume holds fewer of them and the conductivity falls. This is true for acetic acid as for any electrolyte. The quantity that RISES on dilution is the MOLAR conductivity, and for a weak acid it rises steeply, because dilution drives the dissociation forward.

rows.stem:
(a) Write the anode and cathode reactions and the overall cell reaction occurring in a lead storage battery during its use.
(b) Calculate the potential for half-cell containing 0.01 M \(\mathrm{K_2Cr_2O_7(aq)}\), 0.01 M \(\mathrm{Cr^{3+}}\) (aq) and \(1.0 \times 10^{-4}\) M \(\mathrm{H^{+}(aq)}\).
The half cell reaction is
\(\mathrm{Cr_2O_7^{2-}(aq) + 14H^{+}(aq) + 6e^{-}} \longrightarrow \mathrm{2Cr^{3+}(aq) + 7H_2O(l)}\)
and the standard electrode potential is given as \(\mathrm{E^{\circ}}\) = 1.33 V.
[Given : log 10 = 1]
rows.solution:
(a) A lead storage battery in use is discharging, so it acts as a galvanic cell: lead is oxidised at the anode and lead dioxide reduced at the cathode, both giving insoluble lead sulphate.
Anode: \(\mathrm{Pb} + \mathrm{SO_4^{2-}} \longrightarrow \mathrm{PbSO_4} + 2e^-\)
Cathode: \(\mathrm{PbO_2} + \mathrm{SO_4^{2-}} + 4\mathrm{H^+} + 2e^- \longrightarrow \mathrm{PbSO_4} + 2\mathrm{H_2O}\)
Overall: \(\mathrm{Pb} + \mathrm{PbO_2} + 2\mathrm{H_2SO_4} \longrightarrow 2\mathrm{PbSO_4} + 2\mathrm{H_2O}\)
The acid is consumed as the battery discharges, which is why its state of charge can be judged from the density of the electrolyte.

(b) Six electrons are transferred in the half reaction as written, so \(n = 6\), and water is a pure liquid and does not enter the quotient:
\(E = E^{\circ} - \dfrac{0.059}{6}\log\dfrac{[\mathrm{Cr^{3+}}]^2}{[\mathrm{Cr_2O_7^{2-}}][\mathrm{H^+}]^{14}}\)
\(= 1.33 - \dfrac{0.059}{6}\log\dfrac{(10^{-2})^2}{(10^{-2})(1.0 \times 10^{-4})^{14}}\)

The numerator is \(10^{-4}\) and the denominator is \(10^{-2} \times 10^{-56} = 10^{-58}\), so the quotient is \(10^{54}\):
\(= 1.33 - \dfrac{0.059}{6}(54) = 1.33 - 0.059 \times 9\)
\(= 1.33 - 0.531 = 0.799\ \mathrm{V}\)

The hydrogen ion term is raised to the FOURTEENTH power, which is why so modest a change in pH moves this potential so far — the reason dichromate is a strong oxidant only in acid.

rows.stem:
Answer the following :
(a) Low spin tetrahedral complexes are not known.
(b) \(\mathrm{Co^{2+}}\) is easily oxidised to \(\mathrm{Co^{3+}}\) in the presence of a strong ligand [At. No. of Co = 27]
(c) What type of isomerism is shown by the complex \(\mathrm{[Co(NH_3)_6][Cr(CN)_6]}\) ?
(d) Why a solution of \(\mathrm{[Ni(H_2O)_6]^{2+}}\) is green while a solution of \(\mathrm{[Ni(CN)_4]^{2-}}\) is colourless. (At. No. of Ni = 28)
(e) Write the IUPAC name of the following complex : \(\mathrm{[Co(NH_3)_5(CO_3)]Cl}\)
rows.solution:
(a) A low spin complex forms only when the crystal field splitting exceeds the energy needed to pair two electrons in one orbital. In a tetrahedral field only four ligands approach, and none of them head-on along an orbital axis, so the splitting \(\Delta_t\) is small — about four-ninths of the octahedral value for the same ligands. It is therefore almost always LESS than the pairing energy, the electrons stay unpaired, and low spin tetrahedral complexes are not known.

(b) Cobalt is \(3d^7 4s^2\), so \(\mathrm{Co^{2+}}\) is \(3d^7\) and \(\mathrm{Co^{3+}}\) is \(3d^6\). In the presence of a strong field ligand the six electrons of \(d^6\) can all pair into the lower \(t_{2g}\) set, giving an exceptionally stable arrangement with no electron in the high-energy \(e_g\) orbitals. The \(d^7\) ion cannot achieve that — its seventh electron must go into \(e_g\). So a strong ligand makes the \(+3\) state much the more favourable, and \(\mathrm{Co^{2+}}\) is easily oxidised to \(\mathrm{Co^{3+}}\).

(c) Coordination isomerism. Both ions in \(\mathrm{[Co(NH_3)_6][Cr(CN)_6]}\) are complexes, so the ligands can be exchanged between the two metal centres to give \(\mathrm{[Cr(NH_3)_6][Co(CN)_6]}\), a different compound with the same overall formula.

(d) \(\mathrm{Ni^{2+}}\) is \(3d^8\). In \(\mathrm{[Ni(H_2O)_6]^{2+}}\) water is a weak field ligand, so two electrons remain unpaired; a d-d transition is available, part of the visible spectrum is absorbed, and the solution appears green. In \(\mathrm{[Ni(CN)_4]^{2-}}\) cyanide is a strong field ligand and forces all eight electrons to pair in a square planar arrangement, leaving no unpaired electron and no vacancy in the lower set for a d-d transition at visible energies — so the solution is colourless.

(e) One chloride outside contributes \(-1\), so the complex cation is \(+1\). The carbonato ligand carries \(-2\) and the five ammine ligands are neutral, which puts cobalt at \(+3\). Ligands are cited alphabetically, ammine before carbonato. The name is pentaamminecarbonatocobalt(III) chloride.

rows.stem:
(a) What is meant by 'Chelate effect' ? Give an example.
(b) Write the hybridization and magnetic behaviour of \(\mathrm{[Fe(CN)_6]^{4-}}\).
(Atomic number : Fe = 26)
(c) If \(\mathrm{PtCl_2 \cdot 2NH_3}\) does not react with \(\mathrm{AgNO_3}\), what will be its formula ?
rows.solution:
(a) The chelate effect is the extra stability a complex gains when a bidentate or polydentate ligand binds the same metal ion through two or more donor atoms, closing a ring. A chelated complex is markedly more stable than one with the same number of comparable monodentate ligands. For example \(\mathrm{[Co(en)_3]^{3+}}\), in which three ethane-1,2-diamine molecules each close a five-membered ring with the cobalt, is far more stable than \(\mathrm{[Co(NH_3)_6]^{3+}}\).

(b) Iron is \(+2\) in \(\mathrm{[Fe(CN)_6]^{4-}}\), so \(\mathrm{Fe^{2+}}\) is \(3d^6\). Cyanide is a strong field ligand, so all six electrons pair into the lower set, leaving two \(3d\) orbitals empty for bonding.
Hybridisation: \(d^2sp^3\), an inner orbital octahedral complex.
Magnetic behaviour: with no unpaired electron left, the complex is DIAMAGNETIC.

(c) No reaction with silver nitrate means no free chloride ion in solution, so BOTH chlorides must be inside the coordination sphere and there are no counter ions at all. The complex is therefore neutral:
\(\mathrm{[Pt(NH_3)_2Cl_2]}\)

rows.subtopic: Chemical Reactions of Aldehydes and Ketones
rows.stem:
(a) Carry out the following conversions :
(i) Ethanal to But-2-enal
(ii) Propanoic acid to ethane
(b) An alkene A with molecular formula \(\mathrm{C_5H_{10}}\) on ozonolysis gives a mixture of two compounds B and C. Compound B gives positive Fehling test and also reacts with iodine and NaOH solution. Compound C does not give Fehling solution test but forms iodoform. Identify the compounds A, B and C.
rows.solution:
(a)(i) Ethanal to but-2-enal. Two molecules of ethanal undergo aldol condensation in dilute alkali, giving the \(\beta\)-hydroxy aldehyde; heating then dehydrates it to the \(\alpha,\beta\)-unsaturated aldehyde.
\(2\mathrm{CH_3CHO} \xrightarrow{\mathrm{OH^-}} \mathrm{CH_3-CH(OH)-CH_2-CHO} \xrightarrow{\Delta} \mathrm{CH_3-CH{=}CH-CHO}\)

(ii) Propanoic acid to ethane. Heating the acid with soda lime, a mixture of sodium hydroxide and calcium oxide, removes the carboxyl group as carbonate and leaves a hydrocarbon with one carbon fewer.
\(\mathrm{CH_3CH_2COOH} + \mathrm{NaOH} \xrightarrow[\Delta]{\mathrm{CaO}} \mathrm{CH_3-CH_3} + \mathrm{Na_2CO_3}\)

(b) Ozonolysis cleaves the double bond and puts an oxygen on each of the two carbons that carried it, so the two fragments B and C between them account for all five carbons of A.

Compound B gives a positive Fehling's test, so it is an ALDEHYDE, and it also gives the iodoform reaction, so it carries a \(\mathrm{CH_3CO-}\) grouping: the only aldehyde meeting both is ethanal.
\(\mathrm{B} = \mathrm{CH_3CHO}\)

Compound C fails Fehling's test, so it is a KETONE, but still gives iodoform, so it too has a methyl next to the carbonyl. With the remaining three carbons that fixes it as propanone.
\(\mathrm{C} = \mathrm{CH_3COCH_3}\)

Rejoining the two carbonyl carbons into a double bond reconstructs the alkene:
\(\mathrm{A} = (\mathrm{CH_3})_2\mathrm{C{=}CH-CH_3}\), 2-methylbut-2-ene, which has the formula \(\mathrm{C_5H_{10}}\) as required.

rows.stem: An organic compound (A) (molecular formula \(\mathrm{C_8H_{16}O_2}\)) was hydrolysed with dilute sulphuric acid to get a carboxylic acid (B) and an alcohol (C). Oxidation of (C) with chromic acid produced (B). (C) on dehydration gives But-l-ene. Identify (A), (B) and (C) and write chemical equations for the reactions involved.
rows.solution:
Work backwards from the clue that pins one compound down. (C) dehydrates to but-1-ene, so (C) is a four-carbon primary alcohol: butan-1-ol. Oxidation of (C) gives (B), and oxidising a primary alcohol with chromic acid gives the carboxylic acid with the same number of carbons, so (B) is butanoic acid. (A) is the ester of that acid with that alcohol, and butyl butanoate is \(\mathrm{C_8H_{16}O_2}\) as required.

\(\mathrm{A} = \mathrm{C_3H_7COOC_4H_9}\), butyl butanoate
\(\mathrm{B} = \mathrm{C_3H_7COOH}\), butanoic acid
\(\mathrm{C} = \mathrm{C_4H_9OH}\), butan-1-ol

The reactions:
\(\mathrm{C_3H_7COOC_4H_9} + \mathrm{H_2O} \xrightarrow{\text{dil. }\mathrm{H_2SO_4}} \mathrm{C_3H_7COOH} + \mathrm{C_4H_9OH}\)
\(\mathrm{C_4H_9OH} \xrightarrow[\Delta]{\text{conc. }\mathrm{H_2SO_4}} \mathrm{CH_3CH_2CH{=}CH_2} + \mathrm{H_2O}\)
\(\mathrm{C_4H_9OH} \xrightarrow{\mathrm{CrO_3}/\mathrm{CH_3COOH}} \mathrm{C_3H_7COOH}\)

Note that the alcohol must be the PRIMARY butanol: a secondary one would oxidise to a ketone rather than to the acid, and would dehydrate to but-2-ene rather than but-1-ene.
